title: When the Harvest Party Ends
overview: Hosea tells the northern kingdom of Israel that its celebrations are empty because it has turned to other gods, and that exile, hunger and the loss of its children are coming.

parts.label: No joy at harvest (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Israel seems to be celebrating, perhaps at harvest, but Hosea compares them to a prostitute taking payment at the threshing floors. This could mean they paid offerings from the harvest to other gods like Baal, a local fertility god, or that they treated the crops as Baal's payment to them, and either way the threshing floors and winepresses will fail them.

parts.label: Exile and lost worship (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: Driven from the land, they will eat food their law called unclean in Assyria, and their offerings will be as tainted as food from a house in mourning. 'Egypt' likely stands for a return to slavery, and Memphis, a city famous for its huge burial grounds, pictures dying far from home while weeds overrun the homes left behind.

parts.label: Fools and traps (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: Verse 7 may mean the people mock God's true prophet as a fool and a madman, or that the false prophets who promised peace will be shown up as fools when disaster comes. Verse 8 is just as unclear: it may describe traps laid for the true prophet, God's lookout for the nation, or false prophets who are themselves the trap luring Israel into idol worship.

parts.label: Gibeah and Baal Peor (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Gibeah recalls a horrific gang rape and murder in Judges 19, remembered as the depth of corruption. God remembers first finding Israel as a delight, like grapes found in a desert, but at Baal Peor (Numbers 25) they devoted themselves to a Moabite god and became as vile as what they loved.

parts.label: No children, a bitter prayer (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Ephraim, another name for Israel, sounds like the Hebrew for 'fruitful', so the punishment is pictured as the loss of children, and the text says bluntly that they will be killed. Hosea begins to pray, stops as if unsure what to ask, then asks for wombs that miscarry, apparently seeing childlessness as less cruel than raising children only to die in war.

parts.label: Driven out to wander (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: Gilgal was a worship center where Israel made Saul its first king and later worshiped idols, and 'drive them out of my house' may picture exile from the land or a husband sending away an unfaithful wife. The chapter ends with Israel scattered among the nations, which happened when Assyria conquered the north in 722 BC.

think: Do you think fierce anger at someone's betrayal can be a form of love, or does it always mean love has run out?
